plan.contextChunk: This figure shows one undirected weighted graph in which a spanning tree has been picked out by shading. Nine circular vertices carry italic letters: b, c, and d sit across the top, e at the right, f at the lower right, g along the bottom, h at the lower left, a at the left, and i in the middle. Fourteen straight edges join them, each annotated with an integer weight: a-b is 4, b-c is 8, c-d is 7, d-e is 9, a-h is 8, b-h is 11, h-i is 7, h-g is 1, g-i is 6, i-c is 2, c-f is 4, g-f is 2, d-f is 14, and e-f is 10. Eight of those edges, namely a-b, b-c, c-d, d-e, c-i, c-f, h-g, and g-f, are drawn with a broad gray band running behind the line, while the other six remain thin black strokes. The shading is what the reader compares against: it marks an acyclic subset that still reaches every vertex, so the weights along it can be summed and weighed against the heavier unshaded edges it leaves out. The drawing supplies a concrete instance of the wiring problem, in which pins are vertices, possible interconnections are edges, and an edge weight is the amount of wire needed to make that connection.

interactionPlan.concept: A minimum spanning tree is an acyclic set of edges that reaches every vertex with minimum total weight, and different edge choices can yield distinct minimum trees with the same total cost.

demo_steps.title: Read the weighted graph
demo_steps.narration: The picture is an undirected weighted graph: vertices are pins, edges are possible wires, and each number is the cost or length of that wire. The gray bands mark one proposed spanning tree.

demo_steps.title: Build the shaded tree
demo_steps.narration: Step through the highlighted edges from an empty set. Each added edge increases the running total and reaches more vertices while avoiding cycles; after eight edges, all nine vertices are connected.

demo_steps.title: Inspect individual choices
demo_steps.narration: Click any edge to compare its weight with the tree. Heavy unshaded edges such as b-h, d-f, and e-f are left out because they are not needed to keep the graph connected at minimum cost.

demo_steps.title: Compare two minimum trees
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the alternate tree: the highlight moves from b-c to a-h. Because both edges have weight 8, the tree changes but the total remains 37.

state.treeChoice: Alternate tree: swap b-c for a-h

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A minimum spanning tree is about the total cost of a connected, cycle-free edge set, so two different trees can both be minimum when equal-weight edge swaps preserve connectivity and total weight.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use the CLRS-style layout: light-gray circular vertices with black outlines and italic lowercase labels. Place b, c, d across the top; h, g, f across the lower part; a far left, e far right, and i in the middle-left between h and c. Draw all fourteen edges as straight black segments with large serif weight labels near their segments. The current tree should be emphasized by a thick medium-gray band underneath the black edge stroke; in the shown tree the band is on a-b, b-c, c-d, d-e, c-i, c-f, h-g, and g-f. In the alternate view, remove the band from b-c and add it to a-h. Keep selected-edge feedback visually distinct, such as a bright outline or glow plus a small callout, without obscuring the original weights.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Click for selecting any edge: the chosen edge highlights with its weight and whether it is in the shaded tree, making clear how individual edge choices affect cycles, connectivity, and total cost.

authoredContext: We can model this wiring problem with a connected, undirected graph G D .V; E/, where V is the set of pins, E is the set of possible interconnections between pairs of pins, and for each edge .u; _x0017_/ 2 E, we have a weight w.u; _x0017_/ specifying the cost (amount of wire needed) to connect u and _x0017_. We then wish to find an acyclic subset T _x0012_ E that connects all of the vertices and whose total weight w.T / D X .u;_x0017_/2T w.u; _x0017_/ is minimized. Since T is acyclic and connects all of the vertices, it must form a tree, which we call a spanning tree since it “spans” the graph G. We call the problem of determining the tree T the minimum-spanning-tree problem. 1 Figure 23.1 shows an example of a connected graph and a minimum spanning tree.

discrepancies: the default rendering includes a large right-side narration/control panel that is not in the source and compresses the graph to a much smaller left-side footprint rather than using the full figure width
the edge-weight labels have a noticeable white halo/stroke treatment, whereas the source uses plain black numerals directly on the white background
evaluation.notes: The graph topology, weights, vertex labels, gray spanning-tree bands, and overall layout are very faithful, with the main mismatch being the added UI panel reducing the static figure's drop-in resemblance.
action_items: Move the controls below the SVG or make them collapsible so the default view more closely matches the full-width textbook graph.
Remove or reduce the white stroke around the edge-weight labels to better match the source's plain black numerals.
Slightly enlarge the graph within the available canvas when the UI is visible so the node and weight label scale remains closer to the original.
